newsitem.title: CHINA: YEAREND-Asia struggles to feed its growing masses.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-Asia struggles to feed its growing masses.

text.p: The massed humanity of Asia grows relentlessly and the countries with the largest populations are expected to face an increasing struggle to feed their new mouths, agricultural analysts said.

By the end of the century, 60 percent, or 3.75 billion people, of the earth's population will live on this crowded continent, according to U.N. projections, and nearly two thirds of them will be in China and India.

To meet the challenge of feeding them the world is relying on new agricultural techniques to boost crop yields in the Asian countries themselves and the grain exporting giants: the United States, Canada, Australia, Argentina and the European Union.
CHINA BOASTS RECORD GRAIN HARVESTS, BUT IMPORTS SEEN SOARING

Officials in Beijing have announced record grain harvests and pledged that China is able to feed its 1.2 billion people, despite losses caused by floods and droughts and the growing food demands of an increasingly better-off population.
But some economists cast Malthusian predictions about an imminent food crisis and fret over the possibility of a hungry China gobbling up world grain supplies.
Premier Li Peng told the U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit in Rome earlier this year that China would use increased grain yields and exploit more land to maintain food self-sufficiency.
Beijing took steps to boost the harvest by raising government grain procurement prices -- paid to farmers for a set portion of their harvests -- by an average of 25 percent.
Authorities also stepped up efforts at land reclamation and flood and water control.
China has forecast a record grain harvest of 480 million tonnes in 1996, about 15 million tonnes more than last year's bumper yields.

Beijing won accolades from Jacques Diouf, director-general of the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) under the United Nations, who lavished praise on China's agricultural "miracle" and dismissed fears the country would soon be unable to feed itself.
Lester Brown, president of the Worldwatch Institute, a private Washington-based monitor of food supplies, said China was losing cropland at a record rate.
Brown said China's huge population and dwindling water resources had also helped to turn it from a net grain exporter two years ago to the world's second biggest importer behind Japan in 1995.
China must feed more than one-fifth of the world's people on just seven percent of the planet's arable land.
Economic reforms have increased pressure on land use with industrial estates and housing swallowing once productive farm land, prompting authorities to try to curb construction.
By 2000, the country's population is expected to hit 1.3 billion and is seen at 1.6 billion in 2010, pushing grain demand up to 640 million tonnes in that year.
Chinese officials forecast the country's grain consumption to be about 527 million tonnes in the year 2000, against output of about 495 million tonnes.
A growing appetite for meat among increasingly wealthy Chinese has also helped boost demand for grain.
Brown has predicted China's grain imports could soar to well over 200 million tonnes by the year 2030, far above producer nations' current capabilities to supply.
INDIAN FOOD SECURITY CONCERNS GROW AS AGRI INVESTMENT LAGS
India will have to strive hard to attain food security in the coming years in the face of rising population growth but the situation is not yet alarming, officials and analysts said.

"Looking at food and nutritional security we will have to do much more to meet the criterion adopted at the Rome meeting," said S.M. Virmani, a senior official of the Hyderabad-based International Crops Research Institute, an independent research organisation.

Virmani said in the past five to seven years the growth in Indian food production has not been very impressive. Production had hovered around 185 million tonnes with an addition or fall of two or three million tonnes.
"While population is galloping and we have added about 100 million in five years, food production has not gone up correspondingly," Virmani said.
India, with 930 million people, is widely expected to overtake China as the world's most populous country sometime next century.
Virmani said the ratio between pulses and cereals production was also getting wider.
"The Green Revolution (of the 1960s) was restricted to 30-40 districts of the country in the north and south. That area is not getting expanded," he said.
Ashok Gulati, of the independent National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER), said India possessed the technology and what it needed was investment.

"Given the technology unfolding in the next five to ten years, liberalisation of the economy and past performance, we feel India will be reasonably okay after taking care of the population growth," Gulati said.
He said projections made up to 2020 show that in a normal year there would be a net surplus in agricultural production and in years with below normal monsoon there could be marginal surpluses.
"Looking at production trends in the last three years there is no threat to India's food security," said one analyst who did not want to be identified.
"There will be no famine situation. We will continue to be a net exporter in the coming years," he said.
